title: State synchronization across browser tabs
description: Learn how to keep application state consistent across multiple browser tabs. Covers the BroadcastChannel API, storage events, and practical patterns for multi-tab React applications.

data.text: Users often keep the same application open in multiple browser tabs. If each tab maintains its own isolated copy of the state, actions taken in one tab are invisible to the others until a full page reload. Multi-tab synchronization is especially important for authentication state, theme preferences, draft data, and notifications.
This lesson shows how to use browser APIs and React patterns to propagate state changes across tabs efficiently.

`BroadcastChannel` allows different browsing contexts on the same origin to send messages to each other. It is the cleanest modern solution for cross-tab communication because it is explicit, typed, and does not rely on storage side effects.

data.title: BroadcastChannel setup in React
data.content: A custom hook opens a channel on mount, listens for messages, and closes the channel on cleanup.

data.text: Before `BroadcastChannel`, the most common approach was to listen for the `storage` event on `window`. The event fires whenever `localStorage` is modified in another tab. This approach works everywhere but couples your state synchronization to `localStorage` semantics, so it is best used for simple key-value preferences rather than rich application state.

data.title: storage event behavior
items: Fires only in other tabs, not in the tab that wrote the value.
Fires for every key in `localStorage` that changed.
Cannot distinguish between tabs with custom logic.

data.title: Syncing a theme preference with storage events
data.content: The effect listens for `storage` changes and updates local React state when another tab modifies the theme.

data.text: `BroadcastChannel` is preferred when you want a dedicated, typed communication channel. `storage` events are useful as a fallback for simple preferences or when you need to support older browsers. For complex shared state, consider a backend channel such as WebSockets or server-sent events instead of pure browser APIs.

rows: Typed messages between tabs on the same origin
Not available in some older browsers
Limited to string values, fires for every key change
More complex setup, not needed for simple cases
Real-time server-driven updates across all clients

data.title: Don't forget server state
data.text: Cross-tab synchronization only solves the problem within the browser. If a user changes data in another browser or device, you still need polling, WebSockets, or push notifications to stay synchronized with the server.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: BroadcastChannel is the preferred modern API for cross-tab messaging.
Storage events are a simple fallback for localStorage-backed preferences.
Keep cross-tab messages small and explicit; avoid broadcasting the entire application state.
Combine browser-side synchronization with server-side updates for complete consistency.
data.takeaway: Cross-tab synchronization prevents the common bug where a user performs an action in one tab, refreshes another, and sees stale or conflicting data.
